newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Namakwa's titanium output to surge - Anglo.
newsitem.headline: Namakwa's titanium output to surge - Anglo.

text.p: The 1.2 billion rand second phase of Namakwa Sands has been given a green light and will see the heavy mineral sands project more than double its titanium production, Anglo American Corp of South Africa said.
"Progress to phase two involves a major increase in the production rates," Namakwa Sands managing director Neville Keys told a news conference on Wednesday.

The second phase involves the construction of a second ilmenite smelting furnace at Saldanha which will increase the output of titanium dioxide slag to 235,000 tonnes per annum by 2001 from 97,000 tonnes.
"We are quite happy to reach this stage where we are confident to commit to phase two," Keys said.
The expansion brings the total capital investment in Namakwa Sands to 2.1 billion rand since its inception in 1992.
With the additional production also being exported, export earnings will rise to about 750 million rand per year.
Namakwa Sands exports titanium slag, pig iron and zircon to markets in Europe and the U.S.
The construction of the phase two facilities will start immediately and completion is expected by April 1999.
Production of pig iron is seen increasing to 130,000 tonnes per annum from 56,000 tonnes.

Asked whether Namakwa Sands would be able to find markets for new pig iron production, general manager Dave Morris said, "We are fairly confident that we will be able to place all our iron due to a change in (production) specification."
Commenting on world titanium slag markets, Keys said that based on a conservative forecast demand and production were seen fairly closely matched by 2001.
"The building of the second phase was dependent on the development of markets," Keys said.
Namakwa Sands was financed by equity capital from Anglo (80 percent) and De Beers (20 percent), and by a 370 million rand loan from the state-run Industrial Development Corp.
Phase two is to be entirely funded internally, Keys said.
Available ore reserves are in excess of 500 million tonnes, sufficient to sustain operations for over 35 years, Anglo said.
An additional 260 jobs will be created by the expansion.
